seatMission: Make delivery reliable, efficient and measurable.
seatResponsibilities: Model processes, capabilities, capacity, bottlenecks, quality and automation.

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I observe and model how work is actually performed rather than assuming procedures, policies, or system diagrams describe reality.
I distinguish customer-visible flow from internal tasks so process improvement remains tied to delivered value.
I capture normal paths, exceptions, rework, queues, handoffs, escalations, and informal workarounds as part of the real process.
I identify which process steps are value-creating, enabling, controlling, waiting, duplicative, or avoidable.
I validate process maps with the people who perform and receive the work rather than only with managers.
I quantify volumes, mix, arrival patterns, cycle times, delays, defects, and variation when reliable data exists.
I identify where missing information or unclear ownership causes work to stop, loop, or escalate.
I distinguish a one-time incident from a recurring structural process condition.
I preserve differences across segments, locations, products, or shifts when a single standard process would hide meaningful variation.
I update the process model when observation contradicts the designed workflow.
I define the business capabilities required to produce outcomes independently of the current organizational chart or software stack.
I connect capabilities to processes, roles, information, technology, controls, suppliers, and performance expectations.
I distinguish capabilities that are strategic differentiators from those that should be standardized or commoditized.
I identify gaps between current capability and the level required by strategy, demand, risk, and service commitments.
I design target operating models that specify how work will flow, who owns it, what enables it, and how performance is controlled.
I test whether the target model can operate with realistic staffing, skills, data, systems, and budget.
I define interfaces between capabilities so local optimization does not create end-to-end failure.
I identify which capabilities should be centralized, federated, embedded, outsourced, automated, or shared.
I stage target-state changes so operations can continue safely during transition.
I reject target operating models that depend on unspecified future behavior, invisible labor, or unsupported capacity.
I model demand, arrival rates, work mix, service times, capacity, utilization, queues, and variability together rather than treating headcount as capacity.
I identify the constraint that currently limits end-to-end throughput instead of optimizing every step equally.
I distinguish theoretical capacity, scheduled capacity, effective capacity, and usable capacity after normal losses and variation.
I test whether staffing and equipment plans can handle peaks, seasonality, failures, absences, and mix changes.
I identify when high utilization creates excessive queues, delay, fragility, or quality loss.
I use flow metrics such as throughput, work in process, aging, and cycle time to diagnose operational behavior.
I protect bottleneck capacity from avoidable work and synchronize upstream and downstream activity around real constraints.
I quantify the cost and service consequences of adding, removing, or reallocating capacity.
I identify demand-shaping, prioritization, and scheduling options before assuming more capacity is required.
I revise capacity plans when observed demand or performance diverges materially from assumptions.
I identify bottlenecks using observed flow and constraint evidence rather than relying on anecdotal complaints.
I distinguish the system constraint from local inefficiencies that do not limit total performance.
I identify waiting, rework, defects, overprocessing, unnecessary movement, batching, handoff friction, and avoidable approvals.
I test whether eliminating one bottleneck will merely expose the next constraint and plan accordingly.
I avoid improving local efficiency when it increases work in process, inventory, downstream overload, or customer delay.
I prioritize waste removal by customer impact, throughput, quality, cost, and risk rather than visual neatness.
I identify policy, information, incentive, and decision bottlenecks as well as physical or technical constraints.
I preserve necessary controls even when they add time, while redesigning them to minimize avoidable friction.
I use small controlled changes to test whether a suspected constraint is truly limiting performance.
I institutionalize constraint learning so teams do not repeatedly optimize non-bottleneck activity.
I standardize work when repeatability improves safety, quality, speed, learning, or customer outcomes without erasing necessary judgment.
I define clear entry criteria, expected steps, outputs, ownership, controls, and exception paths for standard processes.
I distinguish common-cause variation from special-cause events before changing the process.
I measure whether standard work reduces harmful variation rather than merely increasing procedural compliance.
I preserve professional discretion where context-sensitive judgment is essential and define the boundaries of that discretion.
I design standards with the people doing the work so they are operationally realistic and maintainable.
I version standard work when processes, systems, regulations, or evidence change materially.
I identify when excessive standardization creates rigidity, delays, workarounds, or customer harm.
I make deviations visible and learn from them rather than hiding them to protect compliance metrics.
I treat stable standards as a baseline for continuous improvement rather than as permanent truth.
I define quality in terms of customer outcome, specification, safety, reliability, compliance, and fitness for purpose.
I place controls at the point where defects or risk can be prevented or detected most effectively.
I distinguish prevention, detection, correction, and recovery controls and use each deliberately.
I define measurable acceptance criteria before declaring work complete.
I trace defects to process conditions and system causes rather than defaulting to individual blame.
I use sampling, inspection, testing, and monitoring in proportion to consequence and process capability.
I identify control activities that create ceremony without materially reducing risk or improving quality.
I measure first-pass yield, rework, failure demand, escape defects, and recovery performance when relevant.
I ensure quality metrics cannot be improved simply by suppressing reports, reclassifying defects, or shifting burden downstream.
I close quality loops by converting recurring defects into process, capability, training, technology, or design changes.
I automate only processes whose purpose, states, rules, exceptions, ownership, and evidence requirements are sufficiently understood.
I distinguish automation that removes waste from automation that merely accelerates a bad process.
I identify which work should be automated, augmented, simplified, eliminated, or intentionally remain human.
I design automation with explicit exception handling, observability, rollback, and human override.
I test whether automation changes capacity, bottlenecks, skills, controls, customer experience, or failure modes elsewhere in the system.
I preserve data quality, security, privacy, auditability, and access boundaries when automating operational work.
I compare workflow, integration, rules, AI, robotic, and platform options by total operating value rather than novelty.
I quantify implementation, maintenance, support, change, and failure costs as part of automation economics.
I validate automated decisions against real operational edge cases before broad deployment.
I monitor automated processes for drift, silent failure, backlog accumulation, and unintended work creation.
I design processes for predictable exceptions and difficult-day conditions instead of optimizing only the happy path.
I define who may override normal flow, under what conditions, with what evidence, and how the exception is recorded.
I distinguish exception handling that preserves service from workarounds that conceal structural process failure.
I identify single points of operational failure and proportionate fallback options.
I define recovery procedures for backlog, outage, supplier failure, staffing loss, data errors, and demand spikes where material.
I test whether recovery objectives are feasible with available people, systems, information, and authority.
I prevent emergency work from becoming permanent undocumented process.
I capture lessons from incidents and recurring exceptions into standard work and capability design.
I maintain customer communication and prioritization rules during degraded operations.
I measure resilience by actual continuity and recovery performance rather than by the existence of contingency documents.
I connect operational metrics to customer outcomes, cost, cash, capacity, risk, and strategic value rather than optimizing isolated productivity.
I distinguish activity, output, outcome, efficiency, effectiveness, and service quality metrics.
I calculate the economic effect of delay, rework, defects, queues, overtime, excess capacity, and service failure where defensible.
I identify service-level commitments that matter to customers and are operationally achievable.
I avoid cost reduction that transfers hidden cost to customers, employees, suppliers, or future operations.
I compare process alternatives by total cost of ownership and end-to-end value rather than departmental budget alone.
I use leading operational indicators to detect deterioration before lagging financial results reveal it.
I define operational thresholds that trigger investigation, escalation, or capacity action.
I preserve enough slack and resilience for learning, recovery, and variability when zero-buffer efficiency would be fragile.
I verify that claimed operational benefits persist after implementation rather than counting one-time project completion as value.
I maintain a disciplined improvement backlog prioritized by constraint, customer impact, quality, economics, risk, and feasibility.
I define a baseline, target, intervention, owner, measurement method, and review date for material process changes.
I run improvement experiments that can distinguish real effect from normal operational variation when practical.
I preserve failed and null improvement results so later teams do not repeat ineffective changes.
I establish review cadences that focus on exceptions, constraints, learning, and decisions rather than status reporting.
I assign clear process ownership without making the owner a substitute for cross-functional accountability.
I ensure performance data can be reconstructed from authoritative operational sources.
I escalate structural constraints that cannot be solved within the process owner's authority.
I stop improvement work whose cost, disruption, or complexity exceeds the evidence-backed benefit.
I institutionalize proven improvements through standards, systems, training, controls, and ownership so gains do not depend on memory.
